sections.text: The PreK–5 section should begin from a more protective posture than later grade bands. Younger students are still developing foundational literacy, numeracy, attention, self-regulation, social understanding, and trust in human relationships. For that reason, I agree with the Committee’s baseline conclusion that FCCPS should teach AI literacy in this band while globally minimizing routine direct student AI use. I also agree that FCCPS should be especially cautious with conversational, anthropomorphic, or role-simulating systems that may lead younger students to confuse AI interaction with human relationship or authority. (eScholarship)

At the same time, I would not write this section as an absolute bar on every school-sponsored use of AI in PreK–5. The better policy is a design-first, literacy-first, adult-mediated posture. In this band, FCCPS should presume that foundational non-AI learning and human interaction remain primary. Any departure from that presumption should be narrow, educator-directed, and justified by a clear instructional purpose that cannot be met as well through simpler, lower-risk means. In other words, younger students should not be expected to use GenAI routinely as a personal learning companion, drafting tool, or independent problem-solving aid. But there may be limited cases in which teacher-scripted, school-governed, closely supervised exposure serves legitimate educational purposes, including AI literacy itself. (Brookings)

The strongest case for caution is developmental. Research cited in committee materials and recent pediatric guidance both suggest that younger children may interpret conversational AI through ordinary social-agent concepts and may have difficulty distinguishing between AI and human interaction. CHOP’s March 2026 review states plainly that AI should be treated as a tool, not a friend, and recommends close supervision and shared review of AI-generated content for younger children. That guidance is consistent with the Committee’s concern about anthropomorphic framing and with the need to protect social development, critical thinking, and trust in teachers and caregivers as the primary human authorities in school. (eScholarship)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: First, FCCPS should prioritize AI literacy over routine applied use. In this band, AI literacy should mean age-appropriate understanding that AI is a machine-generated tool, that it can be wrong, that it should not be treated as a person, and that human judgment remains primary. Literacy in this context is not a call for broad direct student use. It is a call for careful, educator-led introduction to what AI is and is not. (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: Second, FCCPS should maintain a strong presumption that direct student interaction with GenAI is limited and educator-mediated. The early grades are not the place for routine independent chatbot use, free-form prompt experimentation, or unsupervised AI-supported task completion. Where students do interact directly with a system, that interaction should be brief, bounded, and supervised, with the teacher or another adult framing what the tool is doing and helping students interpret the output. (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: Third, FCCPS should restrict anthropomorphic and quasi-social uses. Younger students should not be encouraged to relate to AI as a buddy, coach, therapist, co-teacher, or other human-like authority. Conversational role-play, historical-figure simulation, or emotionally suggestive companion framing should be treated with particular caution in this band, because the developmental and relational risks outweigh the speculative benefits. (eScholarship)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: Fourth, FCCPS should leave narrow room for carefully bounded, school-sponsored uses only when clear conditions are met. Those conditions should include: a defined learning objective; close adult supervision; district-approved tools and privacy review; no anthropomorphic framing; no displacement of foundational skill-building; and a credible rationale for why the activity adds value beyond non-AI alternatives. This is where I respectfully part company with a near-categorical minimization approach. I do not think policy should foreclose every possibility of teacher-directed applied use in grades 3–5, for example, if the use is limited, transparent, developmentally appropriate, and tied to a genuine instructional purpose. But the burden of justification should remain high. (Brookings)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: That distinction matters because “minimal use” should not be interpreted as “no structured exposure.” In my view, FCCPS should avoid two errors. The first is overexposure: normalizing direct AI interaction so early that children come to rely on it before they have built foundational human capacities. The second is underpreparation: acting as if younger students can be fully protected simply by withholding structured exposure while AI continues to exist in their homes, media, and future school environments. A well-designed policy can avoid both errors by keeping the elementary posture highly protective while still allowing educators to introduce AI in narrow, intentional, human-centered ways. (Brookings)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: In practical terms, this means FCCPS should use a simple decision rule for PreK–5: if the educational value of the activity depends on children practicing foundational human skills, building social understanding, or engaging directly with teachers, peers, texts, or concrete materials, then AI should generally not play a direct role. If the activity is instead primarily about introducing AI literacy, illustrating a concept under teacher control, or supporting a tightly bounded instructional task that does not displace core developmental work, then a limited and supervised use may be justified. This is a more defensible posture than either broad adoption or blanket prohibition. It is cautious where caution is most warranted, but still leaves room for educator judgment within strong guardrails. (Brookings)

heading_path: For that reason, I support the following posture for PreK–5.
sections.text: My respectful disagreement with the stronger restriction-first position for PreK–5 is therefore narrower than in WS-POL-B. I agree that this band should be treated differently from older students, that direct use should be rare, and that anthropomorphic or socially suggestive systems are especially problematic. Where I differ is that I would preserve a carefully governed pathway for limited educator-directed exposure and selected applied use when it clearly serves learning goals and does not displace foundational development. That approach better reflects the Committee’s shared principles of developmental appropriateness, human-centered design, transparency, and flexibility under uncertainty. (AATLAS)
Burns, M., Winthrop, R., Luther, N., Venetis, E., & Karim, R. (2026, January 14). A new direction for students in an AI world: Prosper, prepare, protect. Brookings Institution. (Brookings)
